name: sun (cosmological concept)

attributes.attribute: a strong natural force read as a god in some myth studies
a goddess whose name may mean sun
the feminine Irish word for the sun

sources: Green, Miranda. Celtic Goddesses: Warriors, Virgins and Mothers. London: British Museum Press, 1995. Pp. 114-115.
Green, Miranda. Symbol and Image in Celtic Religious Art. London: Routledge, 1989, 37.
Hull, Eleanor. Folklore of the British Isles. London: Methuen & Co., Ltd., 1928, 67+.
Monaghan, Patricia. O Mother Sun: A New View of the Cosmic Feminine. Freedom, Calif.: The Crossing Press, 1994.

text: In the 19th century, some scholars read mythology as a kind of poetry made of early stories about nature. The sun was a strong force and an easy god to name. Many scholars looked for a sun link in every story, which brought a backlash against solar mythology. That old attitude still lingers. It hides a false idea, that the sun is always a male figure. Many cultures, from Japan to South America, see the sun as female. The Celts left no text that names a god as the sun. But one goddess, Sul, carries a name that means sun, and the Irish word for sun, grian, has always been feminine. The hero Lancelot and the figure Lugh are raised as sun gods, yet no old text claims this. An honest reading points to the sun as a goddess in Celtic thought. Some scholars now look at this question, but the fear of solar mythology has left it little explained. The same root name also rises in the heroine Gráinne, who shares the sun association.
